scenes.title: 허수는 왜 등장할까?
lines: To record rotation numerically, we first extend multiplication. Squaring an ordinary real number never gives minus one.
We therefore define a new unit i with the rule i squared equals minus one. It is called the imaginary unit.
This does not make i a hidden object inside the game; it is a numerical tool useful for calculating directions.
To see why this rule helps rotation, we will represent numbers as points in a plane.

scenes.title: 아이를 곱하면 왜 90도 돌아갈까?
lines: A complex number a plus bi can represent the point (a,b): the real part is horizontal and the coefficient of i is vertical.
Multiply 2+i by i. The result is 2i+i squared, or -1+2i.
The new point is (-1,2). Its direction turned 90 degrees counterclockwise, while its length remains sqrt(5).
Multiplication by i maps (a,b) to (-b,a), allowing multiplication to represent a planar rotation.
In three dimensions, we also need an axis specifying the plane of rotation. We will connect this directional calculation to a quaternion.

scenes.title: 네 숫자는 세 축과 어떤 관계일까?
lines: A scalar means one number. Here a vector is a three-number group describing a direction, and a component is an individual number in that group.
The symbols i,j,k belong to the three-dimensional rotation algebra. We do not need to draw a fourth physical direction to store four numbers.
For a z-axis rotation, x and y are zero while w and z carry angle information. These are not four independent rotation angles.
Which values produce 90 degrees? We will construct them using a unit axis and familiar trigonometry.

scenes.title: 반각으로 저장해도 회전은 90도
lines: A planar rotation used sine and cosine of the full angle, but our quaternion uses 45 degrees for a 90-degree turn. This needs an explanation.
The difference is how we later apply it: the rotation value multiplies the vector on the left, and its inverse multiplies it on the right.
The complete two-sided operation produces the 90-degree z rotation. A one-sided intermediate is not a physical 45-degree orientation of the object.
For now, distinguish the stored half-angle from the physical turn; we will later calculate both products on the same vector to verify the connection.

scenes.title: 정규화는 방향을 고치는 일이 아니다
lines: Normalization means adjusting the length to one. The length of [3,0,0,4] is sqrt(9+16), or five.
Dividing every component by five gives [0.6,0,0,0.8]. Its squared length is 0.36+0.64=1.
Only the magnitude changed; the axis and component proportions did not. Normalization cannot repair a wrong axis or multiplication order.
Likewise, a faster-moving character does not need a longer orientation value. We will observe speed and orientation separately.

scenes.title: 내적과 외적은 각각 무엇을 묻는가?
lines: The composition formula uses dot and cross products. First distinguish two questions: alignment and the direction determined by their ordered pair.
A dot product multiplies corresponding components and adds them. The dot of (1,0,0) and (0,1,0) is zero, meaning the directions are perpendicular.
A cross product returns a vector perpendicular to both. With our right-handed convention, x cross y is +z, while y cross x is -z.
That order dependence remains in rotation composition. We will read the scalar and vector parts of the Hamilton product separately.

scenes.title: 회전의 절반과 숫자 크기의 절반
lines: We want to apply 45 degrees rather than all 90 degrees. Halving a turn is different from halving all four stored components.
Two 45-degree rotations about the same axis compose to 90 degrees. Our fractional rotation must satisfy that relationship.

A quaternion logarithm converts a chosen axis and half-angle into a convenient vector; its exponential converts that vector back to a unit quaternion. Start with these inverse roles rather than their names.
For z90, the log vector is the z axis times pi/4. Halving it gives a stored half-angle of 22.5 degrees and a physical turn of 45 degrees.
Different chosen axis-angle branches can share a final orientation yet have different intermediate paths. We must choose the path before taking fractional powers.

scenes.title: 같은 벡터로 한쪽 곱과 양쪽 곱을 비교
lines: Our first complex example rotated within a plane using one multiplication. Now rotate (1,0,1) by the same defined z90 turn.
To insert the vector into quaternion algebra, prepend a zero scalar. The rotation is [c,0,0,c], with c=sqrt(2)/2.
Left multiplication alone produces [-c,c,c,c]. Its scalar is nonzero, so it is not the desired pure three-dimensional vector.
Multiplying on the right by the inverse [c,0,0,-c] produces [0,0,1,1]. Removing the zero scalar gives the vector (0,1,1).
The z component parallel to the axis stayed one, while x turned into y. Checking the complete result explains the two-sided multiplication and the half-angle.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 02
lines: Our goal is to record the body's orientation at one instant. Let us first distinguish where the rider is from how the body is turned.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 03
lines: In a plane, two numbers and multiplication could turn a direction. Extending that idea to three dimensions requires choosing an axis; let us examine the numbers we need.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 04
lines: We have separated the roles of the four components. Now we need to construct them from the axis and angle introduced in the preceding lesson.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 05
lines: We have defined a 90-degree turn about z. Returning to the game, we can watch body directions change together; the angle projected by a moving camera is not our defined world angle.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 06
lines: We saw the whole orientation change. What happens if we apply the same 90-degree turn again? We will calculate a fixed-axis example rather than measure a particular game maneuver.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 07
lines: Four turns restored the orientation but changed the signs of its stored components. We must explain that difference to compare orientations correctly.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 08
lines: Different component signs represented the same final orientation. Can that orientation reveal the preceding motion? Let us follow one interval through time.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 09
lines: Final orientation and rotation history are different information. We now need a value that adds no rotation, and will check why initializing every component to zero fails.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 10
lines: The identity value had length one. Other stored rotations use that same convention, so we need to detect drift caused by repeated calculations.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 11
lines: We have checked normalization. To avoid thinking that faster movement needs a longer quaternion, we will observe speed and orientation separately.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 12
lines: Orientation and speed were separate quantities. Let us now undo a stored rotation; the unit-length condition we maintained makes this calculation simpler.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 13
lines: Conjugation undid a unit quaternion. Does the same formula work when its length is not one? A small numerical example will check whether their product is the identity.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 14
lines: We verified that an inverse cancels the original operation. In the game, we will observe a counteracting tilt while separating orientation reversal from reversing the traveled path.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 15
lines: Having undone one rotation, we can now compose two. As multiplication combined planar turns, three-dimensional composition uses a product containing dot and cross products.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 16
lines: Reversing a cross product changed its result. We will now reverse the order of two axis rotations from the same initial direction and inspect the resulting orientations.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 17
lines: The order of fixed-axis rotations changed the result. In the game, watch how turning the body also changes its attached directions; this motivates separating world and body frames.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 18
lines: We have distinguished body and world frames. Now we can ask which extra rotation reaches a target orientation, and verify the answer by applying that delta.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 19
lines: We computed the required rotation difference. To determine how large it is, we will compare all four components and calculate the smallest angle between the final orientations.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 20
lines: The minimum angle measured a difference between orientations. A landing illustrates why distance to the target position and difference from the target orientation are separate questions.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 21
lines: We found the rotation to a target, but applying it all in one frame would produce an abrupt turn. We will first learn to apply a fraction of a fixed-axis rotation.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 22
lines: We can now construct a fractional rotation. To use it, we must apply it to a direction vector; let us check whether the single multiplication used in a plane still works in three dimensions.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 23
lines: Our calculation turned x toward y while preserving the component parallel to the axis. We will now observe body directions separately from the camera frame that projects them on screen.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 24
lines: We have connected stored components to a resulting direction. Reproducing that result in code requires matching the library's component order and coordinate conventions.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 25
lines: With the code conventions established, let us calculate the same input and result ourselves. Rotating and undoing it will verify that the formula restores the original vector.

scenes.title: 연결 해설 26
lines: We completed a rotation and its inverse. Using that result, let us return to our opening question: what do the four numbers store, and which operations do they support?
